docs.text: Smelt ¶ Smelt is a Python tool that aims to greatly simplify shipping native code and standalone applications from Python projects. It covers two related but distinct jobs: A build backend hook : compiling native extensions (mypyc, Cython, Nuitka, handwritten C/Zig) under one pyproject.toml -based API, without any system dependency. This notably covers: Providing a fully standalone way to compile native code in Python projects without any system dependency. Cross-compiling Python C extensions. Combining multiple tools building or providing native code in Python projects (e.g., mypyc, Nuitka, local C/Zig extensions). A bundler : assembling a whole Python application - its dependency closure, compiled extensions, and optionally its own interpreter - into a standalone distribution folder or single file, runnable with or without Python installed on the target machine. Head to Get Started for a minimal build-backend setup - a single mypyc extension declared in a couple of lines of pyproject.toml - or to Bundler: Get Started for a minimal standalone build. Goals ¶ Standalone binary builds - ship your source confidently ¶ The main annoyance when shipping native code is that either you pre-build and host binary wheels for all possible platforms yourself (expensive, and it induces a maintenance load on the infrastructure side), or you ship the source and require users to install the toolchain for your native code themselves - a toolchain that isn't bundled with the interpreter. Native extensions typically require at least a C compiler, and often CMake and/or other build tools. The consequence is that calling pip install on these projects will fail if the toolchain is not installed on the system, breaking the (usual) simplicity of Python package management. Smelt leverages the Zig compiler, which is fully standalone (unlike most C toolchains) and is available as a PyPI package. Smelt implements a Zig-based toolchain to build native extensions (as opposed to most existing solutions which use gcc or clang). This allows shipping your package together with the toolchain to build it, using only standard pyproject.toml config entries. pip install will just work. It also enables some interesting cross-compilation capabilities (for wheels and standalone binaries), although this is still experimental and comes with limitations. Unified, modern pyproject.toml -based interface over several binary backends ¶ Besides hand-crafting native extensions in C, C++, Rust or Zig, there are existing tools in the Python ecosystem to convert Python code to native code. The main issue with them is that they often lack a proper, modern interface in pyproject.toml to use them. They also do not have a unified API. Another issue is that their "public" interface is usually built around a Python -> binary conversion, while internally they are actually Python -> transpiled C -> binary. Smelt provides the following features: Supports Cython, mypyc, Nuitka, and vanilla C/Zig native extensions under one unified pyproject.toml -based API. Isolates the C transpilation from the actual compilation in all of these, and injects Smelt's own Zig-based toolchain, to get truly standalone building (and enable some cross-compilation support). Provides a CLI frontend for developers to easily manipulate them (e.g. toggle native code on and off). Specifically for Nuitka, provides a way to build native extensions module-per-module and have them share a common runtime. Building standalone binaries out of your package ¶ Smelt uses Nuitka to build standalone binaries from Python entrypoints. While Nuitka is designed for that purpose and already capable by itself of doing that, smelt enables the following on top of it: Plugging the pipeline for the other supported binary backends (Cython/mypyc) into Nuitka. Smelt will pre-build the native extensions, and hand the built files to Nuitka (some backends like mypyc generate additional runtime files that are not discovered by Nuitka automatically). Using the Zig compiler with Nuitka ( Note: Nuitka >=4.0.0 now supports the Zig compiler natively, but it was not the case before ) - and thus benefits from its standalone nature. Defining the flags for Nuitka from [tool.smelt.nuitka-binary] , so that the build command is as simple as smelt nuitka-binary . For an application folder (or single file) with bytecode and an optional own interpreter, see smelt bundle first ( Bundler ); the Nuitka route is for a whole-program compile. Where to go next ¶ Get Started - a minimal working setup, one mypyc extension declared in pyproject.toml . Manifesto - the full story behind the problems Smelt addresses, and the reasoning behind its approach. Build Hook - the primary way of using Smelt: plugging it into your pyproject.toml as a Hatchling build hook so native extensions are built automatically whenever your project is built. CLI - the smelt command-line tool, for driving builds manually, producing standalone binaries, and cleaning up build artifacts. Bundler: Get Started - assembling a standalone application distribution with smelt bundle , and its Overview and Reference pages. Advanced Use Cases - cross-compilation support and its current limitations, plus a deep dive into how Smelt makes Nuitka behave as a per-module backend.

docs.text: Advanced Use Cases ¶ Cross-compilation ¶ Smelt provides experimental support for cross-compiling native extensions, leveraging the fact that Zig ships as a single, fully standalone toolchain capable of targeting other platforms without a separate sysroot - unlike a traditional C toolchain, which typically needs a matching cross-compiler and sysroot per target. Building for another platform ¶ Cross-compilation is driven by the -t/--target option of smelt compile : smelt compile my_project.hello --backend nuitka --target aarch64-linux-gnu A comma-separated list compiles the module once per platform, each nested under its own <triple>/ folder (e.g. --target aarch64-linux-gnu,arm-linux-gnueabihf ). Under the hood this passes -target <triple> to zig cc / zig build-lib , the same mechanism Zig itself uses for cross-compiling C/C++ code. Current limitations ¶ Cross-compilation in Smelt is still an experimental, narrow feature - keep the following in mind before relying on it: Supported targets are three Linux triples: aarch64-linux-gnu , arm-linux-gnueabihf (armv7l) and x86_64-linux-gnu . musl, Windows and macOS targets are not supported for extension cross-compilation yet. smelt bundle supports more targets for its interpreter, but a project that declares modules to compile can only be bundled for these three; a project with none can be bundled for any target the interpreter build supports. smelt compile cross-compiles the C each backend emits, not the backend's own code generation. For extensions.c / extensions.zig this makes no difference. For mypyc, the C is generated for the host. smelt bundle -t <triple> cross-compiles the project's extensions fully, code generation included. Nuitka whole-program binaries ( smelt nuitka-binary ) are host-only. The command has no target option. A target pyconfig.h is generated on demand. Building an extension needs a pyconfig.h matching the target's Python ABI; Smelt generates one by running CPython's ./configure for the target (through build-your-python, so the byp extra is required) and caches it. Stability isn't guaranteed. Smelt emits a runtime warning whenever cross-compilation is used; treat produced artifacts as experimental rather than production-ready until this matures. Nuitka internals ¶ Nuitka is one of the binary backends Smelt orchestrates, but it fits the model differently from the others, and that difference drives a fair amount of machinery worth understanding if you rely on extensions.nuitka heavily. The problem: Nuitka is whole-program, not per-module ¶ mypyc and cython treat each module as an independent compilation unit: every module becomes its own extension .so , and any code they all need is factored into a single small shared runtime library (e.g. mypyc ships a …__mypyc runtime the modules link against). Compiling ten modules produces ten thin .so s plus one shared runtime. Nuitka's primary mode of operation is the opposite: it is a whole-program compiler. You point it at an entrypoint and it produces a single artifact (one binary, or one extension module) that embeds everything it needs, including Nuitka's own C "static runtime" - the large body of C code that implements compiled functions, generators, calling conventions, the constants system, and so on. Smelt also exposes Nuitka at the module level, so it can act like the other backends (one native .so per Python module). But because Nuitka has no notion of a shared runtime, naively compiling N modules this way re-embeds that entire static runtime N times - N copies of several megabytes of identical C code. The result is bloated binaries and much longer build times. To be a good per-module backend, Smelt has to build that runtime once and have every module .so link against it - the shared runtime library lib__nuitka_runtime.so . The constants blob, and why it complicates sharing ¶ The one thing that stops the static runtime from being trivially shareable is how Nuitka handles constants . A Python constant - a string literal, a number, a tuple, an interned name like __name__ - is a live PyObject on the heap; it cannot be written as a C static literal, because it only exists relative to a running interpreter. So Nuitka serializes every constant a program uses into a compact binary blob that is embedded in the artifact, and materializes those objects at startup by decoding the blob through the CPython C-API. This is a deliberate optimization over emitting C code that builds each constant: the blob is far smaller, costs nothing to C-compile, and decodes in bulk at import for fast startup. Crucially, this blob is a whole-program structure. It is a set of named sections: one universal section holding the constants every compiled module shares (empty tuple/dict, small integers, common interned names…), plus one section per module holding that module's own literals. At startup each module asks the runtime loader for its own section by name, while the universal constants are decoded once and shared. In a normal Nuitka build there is exactly one blob for the whole artifact, so a single loader that reaches for "the" blob is all that is needed. That single-blob assumption is what breaks when modules become independent units. Each module .so must remain independently importable, so each carries its own blob (its own literals plus a copy of the universal constants). But the runtime code that reads the blob is written around one global accessor - so a single shared runtime would bind to whichever module happened to load first, and every other module would then be handed the wrong module's constants. Merging all modules into one blob is not an option either: that would fuse the modules back into a single unit and defeat the whole point of having independently-importable .so s. How Smelt handles it ¶ The insight is that the coupling is only about data , not code: what must stay per-module is each module's blob and which blob a module reads ; what can be shared is the (large) body of code that reads and uses constants. So Smelt splits the build in two: The shared runtime ( lib__nuitka_runtime.so ) holds the generic static runtime and the universal constants that are identical across all modules. It is compiled once per build and every module links against it (found at load time via an $ORIGIN rpath, so it sits next to the modules in the package). Each module .so keeps its own constants blob and its own generated code, and simply passes its blob into the shared runtime's constants loader. The loader is made blob-agnostic - instead of pulling a single global blob, it receives the caller's blob - so every module reads its own constants while sharing all the surrounding machinery. Concretely this touches only Nuitka's constants entrypoints: the loader ( loadConstantsBlob ) is given the blob pointer as an argument rather than fetching it from the per-module getConstantBlobData , and the module's generated call sites are rewritten to pass their own blob. Everything else - the bulk of the runtime - is compiled once and shared. The net effect matches the other backends: N thin module .so s plus one shared runtime, with the constants of each module kept private to it. Current limitation: packages themselves are not auto-compiled ¶ Auto mode ( extensions.auto.mode = "package" / "all" ) walks a package's filesystem tree and proposes every .py file it finds as a compile target - except a package's own __init__.py , at any depth. This isn't a discovery oversight; Nuitka has no way to do it that fits Smelt's model. Nuitka draws a hard line between compiling a module (point it at a .py file, get a .so ) and compiling a package (point it at the package's directory , which transpiles the whole package - __init__.py and everything Nuitka can see under it - into a single artifact meant to replace that directory as the importable module). Smelt's per-module model, described above, keeps every original source file in place and drops a same-named .so next to it - there is no step where the source is removed. Applying that same model to a package's __init__.py would produce an automode.cpython-*.so sitting right next to the still-present automode/ directory. Python's import system always resolves a name to a package directory before it considers a same-named extension module in that directory, so the freshly compiled .so would simply never be imported - dead weight, silently never taking effect. Until Nuitka's whole-package compilation mode gets its own place in Smelt's model (package in, single replacement artifact out - a different shape from the shared-runtime scheme above), auto mode skips packages entirely and only ever proposes their concrete submodules.

docs.text: Build Hook ¶ The primary way to use Smelt is as a Hatchling build hook. Once configured, every pip install / build of your project automatically compiles the native extensions and entrypoints you declared - no manual step required, and no extra system dependency (Smelt uses Zig as its compiler, which ships as a standalone toolchain through the ziglang PyPI package). Minimal setup ¶ Add smelt to your build requirements, select hatchling as the build backend, and declare the smelt build hook: [build-system] requires = ["hatchling", "smelt"] build-backend = "hatchling.build" [project] name = "my-project" version = "0.1.0" dependencies = ["click"] [project.scripts] my-cli = "my_project.cli:main" [tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel] packages = ["src/my_project"] [tool.hatch.build.hooks.smelt] [tool.smelt] package-dirs = { "my_project" = "src/my_project" } [tool.smelt.extensions] mypyc = ["my_project.fib"] nuitka = ["my_project.cli"] cython = [ { import-path = "my_project.fib_cython", source = "src/my_project/fib_cython.pyx" }, ] [[tool.smelt.extensions.c]] import-path = "my_project.hello" sources = ["src/my_project/hello.c"] [[tool.smelt.extensions.zig]] import-path = "my_project.zighello" folder = "src/my_project/zighello" Every module is compiled to a native .so / .pyd sitting right next to its pure-Python counterpart, which it then shadows - so the rest of your codebase, tooling, and imports don't need to change. Configuration reference ¶ All of the following keys live under [tool.smelt] . The [tool.hatch.build.hooks.smelt] table stays empty: it only enables the hook. Key Type Description package-dirs dict[str, str] Maps a package's top-level import name to the folder it lives in (e.g. {"my_project" = "src/my_project"} ). Used to resolve the import-path s declared below to actual files on disk. extensions.mypyc list of import paths or tables Modules to compile with mypyc . Each entry is a bare import path, or a table with import-path and optional source (path override) and extras . extensions.cython list of import paths or tables Modules to compile with Cython . Same entry shape as mypyc ; source defaults to a .py / .pyx file matching the import path. extensions.nuitka list of import paths or tables Modules to compile with Nuitka , as thin per-module extensions sharing one runtime library. See Nuitka internals . Same entry shape as mypyc . extensions.c array of tables Handwritten C/C++ extensions, compiled with Zig's C compiler ( zig cc ). Each entry has an import-path , a sources list, and extras . sources may also list single-file .zig modules: Smelt translates Python.h to Zig and exposes it as @import("python") (Zig 0.17 has no @cImport ). extensions.zig array of tables Handwritten Zig extensions, built with zig build . Each entry has an import-path , an optional name (library name Zig produces; defaults to the last part of import-path ), a folder (containing a build.zig , defaults to the project root), optional flags passed to zig build , and extras . executables.zig array of tables Executables produced by the project's own build.zig , installed as wheel scripts. Each entry has a name , optional exe , folder , flags and extras . nuitka-binary table Options of the Nuitka whole-program build ( smelt nuitka-binary , see CLI ): extra-flags , zig , include-modules , include-packages , package-data . Per-entrypoint overrides go in [tool.smelt.nuitka-binary.entrypoints.<ep>] , keyed by the [project.scripts] name or an explicit module.path[:func] ; lists append to the project-wide ones, scalars replace. Bundler settings are separate: see [tool.smelt.bundle] in the Bundler: Reference . extensions.auto.mode "off" | "package" | "all" Instead of listing modules by hand, walk the package tree and propose every .py file as a compile target (see limitation below). extensions.auto.backends list of "nuitka" / "mypyc" / "cython" / "bytecode" Backends tried in order, per module discovered by auto mode. Defaults to ["nuitka"] . "bytecode" compiles nothing: the module stays pure Python (shipped as .pyc by smelt bundle , left as source in a wheel). Listing it last means auto mode never fails a build; ["bytecode"] alone compiles nothing. supported-targets list of str Zig-triple patterns ( x86_64-linux-* , *-linux-* , host ). The native build is skipped (not failed) for any target not matching, host included. Also written into the package's manifest, so downstream cross-builds skip it too. Replaces platforms and archs . The hook has no command line: set SMELT_DEBUG (verbose logging) and SMELT_REPORT (path of the auto-mode report, written when the hook completes) in the environment. The CLI reads the same variables; -l/--log-level and --report win over them. extras -gated modules ¶ Any of the module tables above ( extensions.mypyc , .cython , .nuitka , .c , .zig ) accepts an extras list. If any of the listed [project.optional-dependencies] extras isn't installed in the current environment, the build hook silently skips that module instead of failing - handy for optional native acceleration that shouldn't block a plain install: [tool.smelt.extensions] mypyc = [{ import-path = "my_project.fast_path", extras = ["speedups"] }] Auto mode and packages ¶ Auto mode ( "package" / "all" ) currently never proposes a package's own __init__.py , at any depth - only its concrete submodules. This isn't an oversight: see Nuitka internals for why whole-package compilation doesn't fit Smelt's per-module model yet. Configuration location ¶ The hook and the CLI read the same [tool.smelt] table. Settings written under [tool.hatch.build.hooks.smelt] by earlier releases are still read, with a deprecation warning, when [tool.smelt] is absent; having settings in both tables is an error.

docs.text: The primary way to use Smelt is as a Hatchling build hook. Once configured, every pip install / build of your project automatically compiles the native extensions and entrypoints you declared - no manual step required, and no extra system dependency (Smelt uses Zig as its compiler, which ships as a standalone toolchain through the ziglang PyPI package).
docs.title: Build Hook

docs.text: Add smelt to your build requirements, select hatchling as the build backend, and declare the smelt build hook: [build-system] requires = ["hatchling", "smelt"] build-backend = "hatchling.build" [project] name = "my-project" version = "0.1.0" dependencies = ["click"] [project.scripts] my-cli = "my_project.cli:main" [tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel] packages = ["src/my_project"] [tool.hatch.build.hooks.smelt] [tool.smelt] package-dirs = { "my_project" = "src/my_project" } [tool.smelt.extensions] mypyc = ["my_project.fib"] nuitka = ["my_project.cli"] cython = [ { import-path = "my_project.fib_cython", source = "src/my_project/fib_cython.pyx" }, ] [[tool.smelt.extensions.c]] import-path = "my_project.hello" sources = ["src/my_project/hello.c"] [[tool.smelt.extensions.zig]] import-path = "my_project.zighello" folder = "src/my_project/zighello" Every module is compiled to a native .so / .pyd sitting right next to its pure-Python counterpart, which it then shadows - so the rest of your codebase, tooling, and imports don't need to change.

docs.text: All of the following keys live under [tool.smelt] . The [tool.hatch.build.hooks.smelt] table stays empty: it only enables the hook. Key Type Description package-dirs dict[str, str] Maps a package's top-level import name to the folder it lives in (e.g. {"my_project" = "src/my_project"} ). Used to resolve the import-path s declared below to actual files on disk. extensions.mypyc list of import paths or tables Modules to compile with mypyc . Each entry is a bare import path, or a table with import-path and optional source (path override) and extras . extensions.cython list of import paths or tables Modules to compile with Cython . Same entry shape as mypyc ; source defaults to a .py / .pyx file matching the import path. extensions.nuitka list of import paths or tables Modules to compile with Nuitka , as thin per-module extensions sharing one runtime library. See Nuitka internals . Same entry shape as mypyc . extensions.c array of tables Handwritten C/C++ extensions, compiled with Zig's C compiler ( zig cc ). Each entry has an import-path , a sources list, and extras . sources may also list single-file .zig modules: Smelt translates Python.h to Zig and exposes it as @import("python") (Zig 0.17 has no @cImport ). extensions.zig array of tables Handwritten Zig extensions, built with zig build . Each entry has an import-path , an optional name (library name Zig produces; defaults to the last part of import-path ), a folder (containing a build.zig , defaults to the project root), optional flags passed to zig build , and extras . executables.zig array of tables Executables produced by the project's own build.zig , installed as wheel scripts. Each entry has a name , optional exe , folder , flags and extras . nuitka-binary table Options of the Nuitka whole-program build ( smelt nuitka-binary , see CLI ): extra-flags , zig , include-modules , include-packages , package-data . Per-entrypoint overrides go in [tool.smelt.nuitka-binary.entrypoints.<ep>] , keyed by the [project.scripts] name or an explicit module.path[:func] ; lists append to the project-wide ones, scalars replace. Bundler settings are separate: see [tool.smelt.bundle] in the Bundler: Reference . extensions.auto.mode "off" | "package" | "all" Instead of listing modules by hand, walk the package tree and propose every .py file as a compile target (see limitation below). extensions.auto.backends list of "nuitka" / "mypyc" / "cython" / "bytecode" Backends tried in order, per module discovered by auto mode. Defaults to ["nuitka"] . "bytecode" compiles nothing: the module stays pure Python (shipped as .pyc by smelt bundle , left as source in a wheel). Listing it last means auto mode never fails a build; ["bytecode"] alone compiles nothing. supported-targets list of str Zig-triple patterns ( x86_64-linux-* , *-linux-* , host ). The native build is skipped (not failed) for any target not matching, host included. Also written into the package's manifest, so downstream cross-builds skip it too. Replaces platforms and archs . The hook has no command line: set SMELT_DEBUG (verbose logging) and SMELT_REPORT (path of the auto-mode report, written when the hook completes) in the environment. The CLI reads the same variables; -l/--log-level and --report win over them.

docs.text: Any of the module tables above ( extensions.mypyc , .cython , .nuitka , .c , .zig ) accepts an extras list. If any of the listed [project.optional-dependencies] extras isn't installed in the current environment, the build hook silently skips that module instead of failing - handy for optional native acceleration that shouldn't block a plain install: [tool.smelt.extensions] mypyc = [{ import-path = "my_project.fast_path", extras = ["speedups"] }]

docs.text: Bundler: Get Started ¶ A bundler takes a Python application and turns it into something that runs on a target machine without a separate install step - PyInstaller, Nuitka's standalone mode, and PyOxidizer are existing examples of tools that do this in the Python ecosystem. A minimal example ¶ src/greet_demo/cli.py : def main() -> None: print("Hello from a standalone binary!") pyproject.toml : [build-system] requires = ["hatchling", "smelt"] build-backend = "hatchling.build" [project] name = "greet-demo" version = "0.1.0" requires-python = ">=3.12" [project.scripts] greet = "greet_demo.cli:main" [tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel] packages = ["src/greet_demo"] [tool.hatch.build.hooks.smelt] [tool.smelt] package-dirs = { "greet_demo" = "src/greet_demo" } No native extensions declared here - the entrypoint is plain Python, so the distribution ships it as bytecode. This needs the byp extra: $ pip install "smelt[cli,byp]" $ smelt bundle --python own $ ./dist/greet.dist/greet Hello from a standalone binary! The first such build compiles that interpreter, which takes a few minutes; later builds reuse it. Add --onefile on top of either mode to additionally pack the folder into a single file - an executable zip application for byo , a compiled self-extracting launcher for own . docs.text: Bundler: Overview ¶ smelt bundle assembles a standalone distribution for one [project.scripts] entrypoint: the entrypoint's own dependency closure, shipped as compiled extensions plus bytecode, optionally alongside an interpreter. This page covers what it actually does, and where it sits next to existing bundlers. For hands-on usage see Get Started and Reference ; for the vocabulary used below (closure, discovery, payload, tailoring, keep-set) see the Glossary . What gets shipped ¶ Building a distribution starts by computing the entrypoint's closure - every module it needs, standard library and third-party alike - through static analysis, tracing, or both. The non-standard-library part of that closure becomes the payload: each module compiled by one of Smelt's own backends is shipped as the native artifact already produced for it, and everything else is shipped as bytecode ( .pyc ). Nothing here forces a whole-program compile: an application can be built entirely from a mypyc extension, a Nuitka module, and plain Python, and the distribution folder carries the three side by side, exactly as they were compiled for a regular build. byo versus own ¶ The interpreter question is a separate axis from the payload. In byo mode ("bring your own [interpreter]", the default) the folder holds only the application - it runs on any machine with a matching CPython minor version already installed. In own mode, Smelt also builds a CPython interpreter (through build-your-python ) and ships it inside the folder, which then runs where nothing is installed at all. An own interpreter is not simply copied wholesale: by default it is tailored down to the standard-library modules and native libraries the closure actually reaches, plus a small always-kept baseline (see Glossary - Minimal Viable Stdlib) that discovery cannot see on its own. Which parts of OpenSSL, SQLite, libffi , bz2 , lzma or Tk get compiled in follows the same closure - an application that never touches ssl gets an interpreter built without OpenSSL at all, rather than one that has it but never loads it. One folder, one file, or fully static ¶ Either mode can additionally be packed into a single file with --onefile : an executable zip application for byo (no compiler involved - zipimport reads it directly), or a compiled Zig launcher carrying the whole folder, interpreter included, as a compressed payload it extracts on first run for own . The folder is always the thing actually built; packing is a step on top of a finished one, not a second way of assembling one. A further, more experimental axis is how tightly the own interpreter binds to the target's C library. The default own build still dynamically links libc and its own libpython - deliberately, since a portable libc replacement is a much harder problem than a portable Python. On musl targets, --static goes further and produces one monolithic static-PIE executable with no shared libraries of its own at all; getting there requires compiling every native module Smelt would otherwise dlopen() - both stdlib accelerators and Smelt's own extensions - straight into the interpreter, since a fully static binary has no working dlopen() left to load them with later. What this is not: obfuscation ¶ smelt bundle does not transpile or obscure anything by itself. A module shipped as bytecode decompiles about as readily as its source; a module Smelt compiled with mypyc, Cython or Nuitka is exactly as opaque as that backend makes it, independent of the bundler. Anyone relying on a build for source protection should compile the sensitive modules with one of those backends rather than expect the bundling step itself to hide anything. Comparison with existing bundlers ¶ Smelt ( smelt bundle ) PyInstaller Nuitka (standalone mode) PyOxidizer How it assembles the app ships bytecode + whatever native artifacts Smelt's backends already produced freezes bytecode + collects native dependencies via its own analysis/hooks transpiles the whole program to C and compiles it to native code embeds interpreter and modules as in-memory resources in one compiled Rust binary Source protection none by itself - only as strong as the backend that compiled a given module none - bytecode is shipped as-is strong - source is transpiled away entirely strong - no bytecode files on disk Interpreter shipped byo : none, needs a host match. own : built by Smelt, tailored to the app's closure a full, generic copy of a real interpreter Nuitka's own compiled runtime, not a copy of CPython a statically embedded interpreter Compile backend choice per module: mypyc, Cython, Nuitka, or handwritten C/Zig none - doesn't compile Python itself Nuitka only, whole-program none - doesn't compile Python itself Static / libc-independent builds experimental, musl targets only ( --static ) not a target not a target one of its stated goals, though the project has seen little activity since 2023 Smelt also has a second, older way to produce a single native artifact: smelt nuitka-binary , a thin CLI layer over Nuitka's own whole-program compile mode (see CLI ). That command is the one closer in spirit to Nuitka/PyOxidizer's "transpile or embed the whole thing" approach; smelt bundle is closer in spirit to PyInstaller - assemble the app and (optionally) an interpreter, without requiring a whole-program compile.

docs.text: Bundler: Reference ¶ smelt bundle assembles a distribution folder for one entrypoint: Smelt-built extensions plus every other module it imports, shipped as bytecode - and, optionally, an interpreter to run on. See Get Started for a minimal walkthrough and Overview for what each mode actually does; terms like closure, discovery, payload, keep-set and tailoring are defined in the Glossary . Configuration ¶ Settings live in [tool.smelt.bundle] , split into the groups below, and apply to every entrypoint. A single entrypoint overrides them under [tool.smelt.bundle.entrypoints.<name>] with the same keys and groups, <name> being its [project.scripts] name or a module.path:func spec (which also declares an entrypoint that is not a script): [tool.smelt.bundle] python = "own" [tool.smelt.bundle.content] include-packages = ["pkg.plugins"] package-data = { pkg = ["*.json"] } [tool.smelt.bundle.onefile] enabled = true compression = "gzip" [tool.smelt.bundle.entrypoints.greet] python = "byo" Precedence, highest first: command-line flag, bundle.entrypoints.<name> , [tool.smelt.bundle] , built-in default. A scalar replaces the lower level's value; a list appends to it. Unknown keys and wrong types are configuration errors. Every key has a flag named after it: [tool.smelt.bundle.<group>] <key> becomes --<group>-<key> , the prefix being dropped for content and interpreter . Booleans are --x/--no-x , list keys a repeatable singular flag. Run smelt bundle --help for the full text. Command-line only ¶ Flag Description -p, --project Project folder, holding a pyproject.toml . Defaults to . . -e, --entrypoint Entrypoint to bundle. Can be omitted when the project declares a single one. -o, --output-dir Folder the bundle is assembled in. Defaults to ./dist . -t, --target Zig target triple(s), comma-separated or repeated, and/or host . One bundle is built per target; the output is <output-dir>/<script>.dist for a single target and <output-dir>/<target>/<script>.dist when several are built. Defaults to the concrete triples of the most specific supported-targets declared, else host . --no-build Skip the extension build and reuse the artifacts already on disk. -l, --log-level Logging level; logs go to stdout. --report Write a build report to this path. supported-targets (accepted at [tool.smelt] , [tool.smelt.bundle] and entrypoint level) is a list of Zig-triple patterns ( x86_64-linux-* , *-linux-musl ) or host . It has no flag of its own. A target is allowed only if it matches every level that declares the key, so a lower level can only narrow the one above. A requested target outside it is an error, before anything is built. Without -t , the concrete triples (no wildcard) of the most specific declaring level are built; if it only has patterns, or nothing is declared, host is built. General ¶ Key Flag Description python --python Interpreter the bundle runs on. 'byo' (bring your own) ships the application only and needs a matching CPython on the target. 'own' also builds an interpreter and ships it in the folder, so it runs where no Python is installed; the first such build takes several minutes and is then cached per target. Default: byo. optimize --optimize Bytecode optimization level (0, 1 or 2). Defaults to the level this interpreter runs with. Level 2 strips docstrings, which breaks help(), pydoc, doctests and libraries building their help text from docstrings. guard-version --guard-version / --no-guard-version Check the interpreter version in the generated entrypoint. Without it, a mismatched interpreter fails with can't find '__main__' module instead of a readable message. Default: on. isolate --isolate / --no-isolate Add an isolation guard to the generated entrypoint. Without it, running the bundle without -I -S leaves the host's site-packages on sys.path, where it can silently supply a missing module. Default: on. Content ¶ [tool.smelt.bundle.content] Key Flag Description discovery --discovery How to find the modules to ship. 'static' reads import statements, 'trace' imports the entrypoint in a subprocess and reports what it loaded (this runs its module-level code), 'both' unions them. Default: both. include-modules --include-module Force a module into the bundle, on top of what discovery finds. For modules imported dynamically. Repeatable. include-packages --include-package Force a whole package (every module it contains, recursively) into the bundle. For a package that loads its own internals dynamically. Repeatable. exclude-modules --exclude-module Drop a module, and everything under it, from the bundle. For trees discovery reached but that are not needed at runtime. Repeatable. drop-optional-imports --drop-optional-imports / --keep-optional-imports Leave out the modules only reachable through an import whose importer handles the failure itself ( try: import x / except ImportError ). None of them can raise an ImportError by being absent, but what the fallback costs varies: dropping _hashlib saves 5 MB with no visible change, dropping ssl leaves urllib unable to speak HTTPS. Default: keep; the build output lists them either way. package-data --package-data Collect a package's data files into the bundle. Syntax: PACKAGE[:PATTERN,...] (e.g. 'mypkg' or 'mypkg: .json, .yaml'). Repeatable. distribution-metadata --distribution-metadata Collect a distribution's *.dist-info metadata beyond those owning a shipped module. Needed when importlib.metadata is queried for a package whose modules are not themselves shipped. Repeatable. Interpreter ( python = "own" only) ¶ [tool.smelt.bundle.interpreter] Key Flag Description version --python-version CPython release to build the 'own' interpreter from (e.g. '3.12.3'). Only the minor version of the Python running smelt can be shipped, since the bytecode is compiled by it: run smelt under the minor version you want to ship. Default: the supported release matching the running minor version. tailor --tailor / --no-tailor Ship only the standard library modules, extension modules and libraries the application was found to need, instead of all of them. Keeps an 'own' bundle a reasonable size, but a module reached only through a name absent from the source is invisible to discovery and becomes a runtime ImportError: put it back with --include-module. Each distinct set of disabled libraries needs its own interpreter build (minutes), cached separately. Default: tailored. drop-stdlib-groups --drop-stdlib-group Ship the 'own' interpreter without an optional group of the minimal standard library (currently: international_hostnames, 1.1 MB, which costs support for non-ASCII hostnames). Refused for groups nothing can run without. Repeatable. static --static / --no-static Build one monolithic, static-PIE 'own' interpreter (no libpythonX.Y.so) instead of the dynamic shape. A static interpreter has no working dlopen(), so every native module has to be compiled into it: --static-module for standard library modules, --inittab for smelt's own extensions. Any .so left in the bundle fails the build. Verified only for x86_64-linux-musl. Default: off. static-modules --static-module With --static, compile a standard library module (e.g. '_socket', 'zlib') into the interpreter as a builtin. Repeatable. inittab --inittab / --no-inittab With the 'own' interpreter, link smelt's own compiled extensions into it instead of shipping .so files, which skips dlopen() and RPATH for them. This replaces the interpreter's own entrypoint, and a bad build has no .so fallback. Experimental. Default: off. Onefile ¶ [tool.smelt.bundle.onefile] Key Flag Description enabled --onefile / --no-onefile Also pack the finished folder into a single file. With 'byo' that is an executable zip application (a /bin/sh preamble locating a CPython, followed by a zip). With 'own' it is a compiled launcher carrying the whole folder, interpreter included, as a compressed payload it unpacks into a cache directory on first run. Default: off. compression --onefile-compression Payload compression. 'xz' (default) is smallest and slowest to inflate on the first run, 'gzip' trades size for speed, 'none' stores it as is. A 'byo' payload is imported straight out of its zip, so it is deflated for 'xz' and 'gzip' alike. compression-preset --onefile-compression-preset Compression preset: 0-9 for xz, 1-9 for gzip. Default: 6. Higher presets shrink the file but cost build time and first-run inflation time. cache --onefile-cache / --no-onefile-cache Reuse a previous extraction found in the cache directory instead of always re-extracting. Set SMELT_ONEFILE_VERBOSE=1 on the built artifact to see the decision at runtime. Default: on. keep-folder --onefile-keep-folder / --onefile-only Keep the distribution folder once it is packed (default). --onefile-only deletes it and leaves only the single file, for a job that publishes one artifact. Requires --onefile. Isolated build (experimental) ¶ [tool.smelt.bundle.isolated-build] Key Flag Description enabled --isolated-build / --no-isolated-build Experimental. Reinstall every third-party native dependency for the target instead of copying the build installed here. Needs the 'isolated-build' extra and a network fetch per native dependency. Default: off. versions --isolated-build-versions Which version of each dependency --isolated-build fetches: 'local' (the one installed here, default) or 'pyproject' (as declared in [project.dependencies]).

docs.title: Bundler: Reference

docs.text: Settings live in [tool.smelt.bundle] , split into the groups below, and apply to every entrypoint. A single entrypoint overrides them under [tool.smelt.bundle.entrypoints.<name>] with the same keys and groups, <name> being its [project.scripts] name or a module.path:func spec (which also declares an entrypoint that is not a script): [tool.smelt.bundle] python = "own" [tool.smelt.bundle.content] include-packages = ["pkg.plugins"] package-data = { pkg = ["*.json"] } [tool.smelt.bundle.onefile] enabled = true compression = "gzip" [tool.smelt.bundle.entrypoints.greet] python = "byo" Precedence, highest first: command-line flag, bundle.entrypoints.<name> , [tool.smelt.bundle] , built-in default. A scalar replaces the lower level's value; a list appends to it. Unknown keys and wrong types are configuration errors. Every key has a flag named after it: [tool.smelt.bundle.<group>] <key> becomes --<group>-<key> , the prefix being dropped for content and interpreter . Booleans are --x/--no-x , list keys a repeatable singular flag. Run smelt bundle --help for the full text.
docs.title: Configuration

docs.text: Flag Description -p, --project Project folder, holding a pyproject.toml . Defaults to . . -e, --entrypoint Entrypoint to bundle. Can be omitted when the project declares a single one. -o, --output-dir Folder the bundle is assembled in. Defaults to ./dist . -t, --target Zig target triple(s), comma-separated or repeated, and/or host . One bundle is built per target; the output is <output-dir>/<script>.dist for a single target and <output-dir>/<target>/<script>.dist when several are built. Defaults to the concrete triples of the most specific supported-targets declared, else host . --no-build Skip the extension build and reuse the artifacts already on disk. -l, --log-level Logging level; logs go to stdout. --report Write a build report to this path. supported-targets (accepted at [tool.smelt] , [tool.smelt.bundle] and entrypoint level) is a list of Zig-triple patterns ( x86_64-linux-* , *-linux-musl ) or host . It has no flag of its own. A target is allowed only if it matches every level that declares the key, so a lower level can only narrow the one above. A requested target outside it is an error, before anything is built. Without -t , the concrete triples (no wildcard) of the most specific declaring level are built; if it only has patterns, or nothing is declared, host is built.
docs.title: Command-line only

docs.text: Key Flag Description python --python Interpreter the bundle runs on. 'byo' (bring your own) ships the application only and needs a matching CPython on the target. 'own' also builds an interpreter and ships it in the folder, so it runs where no Python is installed; the first such build takes several minutes and is then cached per target. Default: byo. optimize --optimize Bytecode optimization level (0, 1 or 2). Defaults to the level this interpreter runs with. Level 2 strips docstrings, which breaks help(), pydoc, doctests and libraries building their help text from docstrings. guard-version --guard-version / --no-guard-version Check the interpreter version in the generated entrypoint. Without it, a mismatched interpreter fails with can't find '__main__' module instead of a readable message. Default: on. isolate --isolate / --no-isolate Add an isolation guard to the generated entrypoint. Without it, running the bundle without -I -S leaves the host's site-packages on sys.path, where it can silently supply a missing module. Default: on.
docs.title: General

docs.text: [tool.smelt.bundle.content] Key Flag Description discovery --discovery How to find the modules to ship. 'static' reads import statements, 'trace' imports the entrypoint in a subprocess and reports what it loaded (this runs its module-level code), 'both' unions them. Default: both. include-modules --include-module Force a module into the bundle, on top of what discovery finds. For modules imported dynamically. Repeatable. include-packages --include-package Force a whole package (every module it contains, recursively) into the bundle. For a package that loads its own internals dynamically. Repeatable. exclude-modules --exclude-module Drop a module, and everything under it, from the bundle. For trees discovery reached but that are not needed at runtime. Repeatable. drop-optional-imports --drop-optional-imports / --keep-optional-imports Leave out the modules only reachable through an import whose importer handles the failure itself ( try: import x / except ImportError ). None of them can raise an ImportError by being absent, but what the fallback costs varies: dropping _hashlib saves 5 MB with no visible change, dropping ssl leaves urllib unable to speak HTTPS. Default: keep; the build output lists them either way. package-data --package-data Collect a package's data files into the bundle. Syntax: PACKAGE[:PATTERN,...] (e.g. 'mypkg' or 'mypkg: .json, .yaml'). Repeatable. distribution-metadata --distribution-metadata Collect a distribution's *.dist-info metadata beyond those owning a shipped module. Needed when importlib.metadata is queried for a package whose modules are not themselves shipped. Repeatable.
docs.title: Content

docs.text: [tool.smelt.bundle.interpreter] Key Flag Description version --python-version CPython release to build the 'own' interpreter from (e.g. '3.12.3'). Only the minor version of the Python running smelt can be shipped, since the bytecode is compiled by it: run smelt under the minor version you want to ship. Default: the supported release matching the running minor version. tailor --tailor / --no-tailor Ship only the standard library modules, extension modules and libraries the application was found to need, instead of all of them. Keeps an 'own' bundle a reasonable size, but a module reached only through a name absent from the source is invisible to discovery and becomes a runtime ImportError: put it back with --include-module. Each distinct set of disabled libraries needs its own interpreter build (minutes), cached separately. Default: tailored. drop-stdlib-groups --drop-stdlib-group Ship the 'own' interpreter without an optional group of the minimal standard library (currently: international_hostnames, 1.1 MB, which costs support for non-ASCII hostnames). Refused for groups nothing can run without. Repeatable. static --static / --no-static Build one monolithic, static-PIE 'own' interpreter (no libpythonX.Y.so) instead of the dynamic shape. A static interpreter has no working dlopen(), so every native module has to be compiled into it: --static-module for standard library modules, --inittab for smelt's own extensions. Any .so left in the bundle fails the build. Verified only for x86_64-linux-musl. Default: off. static-modules --static-module With --static, compile a standard library module (e.g. '_socket', 'zlib') into the interpreter as a builtin. Repeatable. inittab --inittab / --no-inittab With the 'own' interpreter, link smelt's own compiled extensions into it instead of shipping .so files, which skips dlopen() and RPATH for them. This replaces the interpreter's own entrypoint, and a bad build has no .so fallback. Experimental. Default: off.
docs.title: Interpreter (python = "own" only)

docs.text: [tool.smelt.bundle.onefile] Key Flag Description enabled --onefile / --no-onefile Also pack the finished folder into a single file. With 'byo' that is an executable zip application (a /bin/sh preamble locating a CPython, followed by a zip). With 'own' it is a compiled launcher carrying the whole folder, interpreter included, as a compressed payload it unpacks into a cache directory on first run. Default: off. compression --onefile-compression Payload compression. 'xz' (default) is smallest and slowest to inflate on the first run, 'gzip' trades size for speed, 'none' stores it as is. A 'byo' payload is imported straight out of its zip, so it is deflated for 'xz' and 'gzip' alike. compression-preset --onefile-compression-preset Compression preset: 0-9 for xz, 1-9 for gzip. Default: 6. Higher presets shrink the file but cost build time and first-run inflation time. cache --onefile-cache / --no-onefile-cache Reuse a previous extraction found in the cache directory instead of always re-extracting. Set SMELT_ONEFILE_VERBOSE=1 on the built artifact to see the decision at runtime. Default: on. keep-folder --onefile-keep-folder / --onefile-only Keep the distribution folder once it is packed (default). --onefile-only deletes it and leaves only the single file, for a job that publishes one artifact. Requires --onefile.
docs.title: Onefile

docs.text: [tool.smelt.bundle.isolated-build] Key Flag Description enabled --isolated-build / --no-isolated-build Experimental. Reinstall every third-party native dependency for the target instead of copying the build installed here. Needs the 'isolated-build' extra and a network fetch per native dependency. Default: off. versions --isolated-build-versions Which version of each dependency --isolated-build fetches: 'local' (the one installed here, default) or 'pyproject' (as declared in [project.dependencies]).

docs.text: CLI ¶ Installing Smelt with the cli extra ( pip install "smelt[cli]" ) provides the smelt command-line tool. It exposes everything the build hook does, but callable directly - useful outside of a Hatchling build (e.g. producing a standalone binary, or driving a [tool.smelt] -configured build from a script or CI job). $ smelt --help Usage: smelt [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]... Entrypoint for Smelt frontend Options: -p, --project EXISTING_PATH Project to act on: a folder holding a pyproject.toml. Default: the current folder. -l, --log-level [critical|fatal|error|warn|warning|info|debug|notset] Logging level to apply. Logs are emitted to stdout. --report TEXT Write a report to the given path. --help Show this message and exit. Commands: build Builds the extensions declared in the project's Smelt... bundle Assembles a bundle for an entrypoint: smelt-built... clean Deletes built dynlibs (and their mypyc runtime, where... compile One-off compile of a single installed module with the... config Shows the resolved config: the project-wide settings,... nuitka-binary Builds a Nuitka whole-program executable per entrypoint,... -p/--project , -l/--log-level and --report are options of the smelt group, so they go before the command: smelt -p path/to/project bundle . Every command reads its configuration from a pyproject.toml , from [tool.smelt] (see Build Hook ). nuitka-binary ¶ The headline feature of Smelt's CLI: compiles a [project.scripts] entrypoint (and everything it imports) into a single, fully standalone executable via Nuitka, with no interpreter or system dependency required on the target machine. $ smelt nuitka-binary --help Usage: smelt nuitka-binary [OPTIONS] Builds a Nuitka whole-program executable per entrypoint, configured by [tool.smelt.nuitka-binary]. Options: -e, --entrypoint TEXT Restrict the build to this entrypoint: either its script name as declared in [project.scripts] (e.g. 'afpu'), or its 'module.path'/'module.path:func_name' key as declared in [tool.smelt.nuitka-binary.entrypoints]. Builds all configured entrypoints if omitted. --package-data TEXT Collect a package's data files into the binary, on top of [tool.smelt.nuitka-binary] package-data. Syntax: PACKAGE[:PATTERN,...] (e.g. 'mypkg:*.json,*.yaml'). Repeatable. --no-cache Disable Nuitka's build cache, forcing a full rebuild. --help Show this message and exit. Without -e/--entrypoint , every entrypoint declared in [project.scripts] (plus any declared under [tool.smelt.nuitka-binary.entrypoints] or [tool.smelt.bundle.entrypoints] ) is built. Options live in [tool.smelt.nuitka-binary] , which is independent from [tool.smelt.bundle] ; [tool.smelt.nuitka-binary.entrypoints.<ep>] overrides them per entrypoint (scalars replace, lists append): [tool.smelt.nuitka-binary] extra-flags = ["--lto=yes"] # passed to Nuitka as is zig = true # compile with Smelt's Zig toolchain (default) include-modules = ["pkg.plugins.a"] # modules Nuitka's import-follower can't see include-packages = ["pkg.plugins"] package-data = { pkg = ["*.json"] } # data files collected from a package [tool.smelt.nuitka-binary.entrypoints.greet] extra-flags = ["--onefile"] --package-data PACKAGE[:PATTERN,...] adds to package-data for the run. The former --embed-file is deprecated in favor of it. This compiles the whole program to native code via Nuitka. For an application that assembles bytecode and compiled extensions into a distribution folder instead - optionally with its own bundled interpreter - see bundle below, and the Bundler section. bundle ¶ Smelt's other route to a standalone application: assembles a distribution folder for one entrypoint out of Smelt-built extensions plus bytecode for everything else it imports, and optionally an interpreter to run on. Settings come from [tool.smelt.bundle] ; every one of them also has a flag. See Bundler: Get Started for a walkthrough and Bundler: Reference for the full list. $ smelt bundle --help Usage: smelt bundle [OPTIONS] Assembles a bundle for an entrypoint: smelt-built extensions plus every other module it imports, shipped as bytecode. With `--python byo` (the default) the result runs on any machine with a matching CPython installed. With `--python own` the interpreter is built and shipped in the folder too, which then runs on a machine with no Python at all. build ¶ Builds every native extension declared in the Smelt config ( extensions.mypyc , .cython , .nuitka , .c , .zig ) for the project, without touching entrypoints. This is what the build hook runs automatically during a Hatchling build; use this command to run the same step manually, e.g. for a project configured via plain [tool.smelt] , or to rebuild extensions in place during local development. $ smelt build clean ¶ Deletes the native artifacts Smelt built (and their mypyc runtime, where applicable) for a project, unshadowing each module's .py source back to being the one Python imports. Useful to reset a development checkout back to pure Python. $ smelt clean [--shadowed-only] --shadowed-only only cleans modules with a pure-Python fallback to unshadow, excluding handwritten C/Zig extensions. config ¶ Prints the resolved config: the project-wide settings, then the bundler settings of every entrypoint, each followed by the level it came from ( default , a pyproject table, or cli ). Use it to debug precedence between [tool.smelt.bundle] and its per-entrypoint overrides. compile ¶ smelt compile MODULE_IMPORT_PATH compiles a single installed module with a chosen backend ( -b/--backend mypyc|nuitka|cython ), optionally cross-compiling it for one or more platforms ( -t/--target , Zig triples or host , comma-separated, see Advanced Use Cases ). Mainly for trying a backend on one module. Renamed commands ¶ The 0.7 command names still work as hidden aliases that print a deprecation line, and are removed in 0.9: show-config ( config ), build-extensions ( build ), build-standalone-binary ( nuitka-binary ), compile-module ( compile ), clean-artifacts ( clean ). Their project/logging/report options keep their old spelling when used through the alias. smelt nuitkaify ENTRYPOINT moved to python -m smelt.nuitkaify ENTRYPOINT .

docs.text: Get Started ¶ Install Smelt and Hatchling as build requirements, and declare a mypyc module to compile - here, a plain recursive fib function: src/fib_demo/fib.py : def fib(n: int) -> int: if n <= 1: return n return fib(n - 2) + fib(n - 1) pyproject.toml : [build-system] requires = ["hatchling", "smelt"] build-backend = "hatchling.build" [project] name = "fib-demo" version = "0.1.0" requires-python = ">=3.12" [tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel] packages = ["src/fib_demo"] [tool.hatch.build.hooks.smelt] [tool.smelt] package-dirs = { "fib_demo" = "src/fib_demo" } [tool.smelt.extensions] mypyc = ["fib_demo.fib"] That's it - no hello.c , no manual setup.py . Building the project (e.g. pip install . , or python -m build ) compiles fib.py with mypyc and drops a native fib*.so right next to it, which then shadows the pure-Python source: import fib_demo.fib transparently loads the compiled extension. See Build Hook for the full configuration reference (mypyc, Cython, Nuitka, and handwritten C/Zig extensions), and CLI for driving builds outside of a Hatchling build. Basic commands ¶ Installing Smelt with the cli extra ( pip install "smelt[cli]" ) also gives you the smelt command, which can drive the same fib-demo project by hand - handy to inspect or rebuild extensions without going through a full pip install / build . smelt --help lists every available command; see CLI for the full reference. A few of them, run from the fib-demo project root: smelt config parses pyproject.toml and prints the config Smelt actually resolved, with the source of each bundler setting - useful to confirm your extensions declarations were picked up correctly: $ smelt config [tool.smelt] package-dirs = {fib_demo = "src/fib_demo"} supported-targets = (not set) extensions.mypyc = [{import-path = "fib_demo.fib"}] extensions.cython = [] ... A project with [project.scripts] entries also gets a "Bundler settings" block per entrypoint, each value tagged with where it came from ( default , a pyproject.toml table, or the command line). smelt build runs the same compilation step the build hook runs during pip install / build , without needing a full build. For fib-demo this compiles fib.py with mypyc and drops two files next to it: the compiled module itself, and its small mypyc runtime: $ smelt build $ ls src/fib_demo __init__.py fib.cpython-312-x86_64-linux-gnu.so fib__mypyc.cpython-312-x86_64-linux-gnu.so fib.py fib.py is still there, but it's now shadowed: import fib_demo.fib loads the compiled .so , not the source file. smelt clean reverses that: it deletes the compiled .so s (and the mypyc runtime alongside them), unshadowing fib.py back to being the one Python imports - handy to reset a checkout to pure Python: $ smelt clean Deleted following artifacts: fib_demo.fib: - src/fib_demo/fib.cpython-312-x86_64-linux-gnu.so (was shadowing src/fib_demo/fib.py) - src/fib_demo/fib__mypyc.cpython-312-x86_64-linux-gnu.so

docs.text: Glossary ¶ The vocabulary used by Smelt's application bundler ( smelt bundle ) and by the code that implements it. Defined here once; the modules involved point back at this page rather than re-explaining the terms. Closure ¶ The set of Python modules an entrypoint needs at runtime, computed as the transitive closure of the "imports" relation starting from that entrypoint. That is the mathematical sense of the word: start with the entrypoint module, add everything it imports, then everything those import, and repeat until nothing new appears. Implemented by smelt.dist.collect_closure , which returns {import_path: ResolvedModule} . What it contains: every module, not every distribution. A closure is a set of import paths ( click.core , json.decoder , _ssl ), not a list of packages from pyproject.toml . A dependency list says what to install; a closure says what is imported. The two differ a lot: a distribution with no dependencies of its own still reaches deep into the standard library. the standard library and third-party code alike , each entry classified by smelt.explorer.ResolvedModule — its kind (source, extension module, namespace package, builtin, frozen, unresolvable), its file on disk, and whether it belongs to the standard library. the packages its members live under. Importing a.b.c also imports a and a.b , so those are in the closure even when nothing names them directly. How it is computed — DiscoveryMode , one of: static : parse each module and follow the import statements found anywhere in its AST, including inside functions and conditional branches; trace : import the entrypoint in a subprocess and record what actually landed in sys.modules ; both (the default): the union of the two. A closure is an estimate, in both directions ¶ This matters more than the definition, and it is why include-modules and exclude-modules exist: it can miss modules. An import performed on a computed name ( importlib.import_module("plugins." + name) ), from a plugin registry, or lazily on a code path not taken during tracing, is invisible. Name those with include-modules / include-packages , exactly as Nuitka requires for the same reason. it can include modules that are never used. The static walk follows imports written inside functions, which is correct for application code (a lazy import is a real dependency) but pulls in far too much from the standard library, whose modules reference each other from rarely-taken helpers. docs.text: Manifesto ¶ The problem with Python projects distribution ¶ One usual headache with Python is software distribution. As an interpreted language, Python has some limitations compared to other compiled languages - first because shipping your Python code requires an interpreter on the target machine, and second because the dynamic nature of the language makes obfuscation difficult - which is a problem for closed-source projects. Regarding the distribution issue, one simple solution is to ship an entire interpreter together with the project, in order to make it a standalone binary. That's what tools like PyInstaller do, for example. It has limitations though: It tends to produce bloated binaries, as the entire interpreter is shipped, even though only a tiny part of the standard library might be used by the shipped project. It does not obfuscate anything, as the source code is shipped directly; even if one were to only ship the compiled .pyc files, these still leak most of the information if it has not been pre-processed by obfuscation tools. As a consequence, it's not uncommon to see Python-to-C transpilers such as Nuitka being used for the sake of obfuscating, or to produce less bloated binaries. Transpiling to C actually allows eliminating dead code and also provides actual obfuscation - but it also makes the platform-specific part more complex, as now the whole project needs to be compiled for the target platform - whereas methods based on interpreter bundling only have to bundle a pre-built interpreter binary for the target platform, the pure Python code itself being portable. Another dimension to that problem appears when one starts using native code in their Python project - native code being usually some kind of C extension (or other languages such as Rust or Zig). That native code also needs to be built per platform - even when an interpreter is already available on the target host. Packages that have native code will be built into platform-specific wheels; for major libraries, these wheels are usually pre-built and uploaded to the PyPI index, which means you often don't have to deal with that as a user of the library. However, for smaller projects (or closed-source ones) that might not have a complex multi-platform build pipeline, people installing the library might have to compile the project locally. Compiling the native code usually implies dependency on the host system (at least a C compiler!), which might not be met all the time. Add to that the fact there are now multiple tools that can provide native code in Python projects: standard C extensions, Rust extensions, mypyc-compiled modules, Nuitka-compiled modules, etc. These tools all have independent build tools and pipelines, which are themselves covered by multiple layers of abstraction in the Python build backend. That makes handling cross-platform distribution (and even single-platform ones!) considerably more complex than it would be with a compiled programming language. Smelt's key ingredients ¶ Smelt aims to solve these problems along 4 axes: Making native code building completely self-contained by removing system dependencies (such as a C compiler) from the equation, thus making a simple pip install ... enough to install a package with native code. This is achieved by leveraging Zig as the compiler backend: Zig ships as a fully standalone, self-contained toolchain, and is itself available as a PyPI package ( ziglang ). Orchestrating the aforementioned native code solutions under one single interface, to allow automating the build of complex projects from a simple config file. Smelt provides a unified, modern, pyproject.toml -based API on top of several existing Python-to-binary tools: mypyc, Cython, Nuitka, and handwritten C/Zig extensions. Providing a self-contained cross-compiling solution for native code within Python projects, which is for now largely absent from the Python ecosystem. Providing standalone binary builds (a single executable for an entire Python application) as a first-class citizen - with all the features mentioned in the bullet points above.
